items.question: As a performance engineer with dozens of patents and three decades of infrastructure design experience I would respectfully disagree.  A small cache SRAM design will only improve latency when operating queue lengths (batch sizes) are short.  Latency for any request is a function of service time plus queueing time.  For a Cerebras system with low service time, batch sizes must be kept short to deliver rapid latency.  Agents are numerous (10x+ more than humans) and will flood concurrent requests to a Cerebras platform, generating very long queue lengths, thus total wait times will suffer.  A Cerebras system can only produce short latencies when the number of requests (batch size) is limited.  This is the classic fast response time vs. large batch size high-throughput design point.  An F1 car has much shorter latency than a bus.  But if one wants to move 50 people from point A to point B an F1 car is a very long latency solution.

items.question:
I am not particularly comfortable with financing or accounting matters because, you know, I am "just" an engineer. But my simple understanding is that the senior analysts who predict a semiconductor industry crash, base their reasoning in the impossibility of indefinite hyperscaler capex growth. 

They claim that in the best scenario, capex will reach a plateau, possibly around 2027. These analysts are generally engineering illiterates and do not care about or understand technological challenges, but they still acknowledge that price per token and performance per watt or invested dollar will steadily improve over the next product generations, which will materially improve economics. 

However, more performance per invested dollar actually goes in the oposite direction of more capex, as less money is required to get more raw performance. Thus capex growth may not be required.

Since the semiconductor industry revenue is directly related with hyperscaler capex, a stall of capex growth will stop or reduce semiconductor revenue growth. Eventually, stock prices of companies in the AI hardware business will return to normal multiples. 

This is supposed to be the best scenario of said analysts.

In my opinion, it is a given that at some point capex growth will be significantly reduced. In that sense, I agree with these analysts. What we do not know is when. I am not talking about absolute capex on any given year, but about capex /growth/ over the years.

I think that, after the recent semiconductor sell off, we need to figure out whether current stock prices already reflect normal multiples based on moderatelly growing capex over the next few years, or we are still pricing impossible capex growth over the next 10 years, so a heavier correction is eventually coming.

Focusing purely on raw FLOPS misses the actual physical wall hitting AI data centers today ⚡. The energy cost of dragging bits across copper traces dwarfs the energy spent on actual matrix math. Moving data isn't just an efficiency nuisance. It's an onto-causal bottleneck where electrical resistance burns watts before computation even begins 🧠.

True scaling up to 2035 won't come from larger GPU dies or bigger clusters. It demands a collapse of the memory-compute boundary itself 🔬. The data movement barrier isn't a permanent physical law. It's an artifact of forcing continuous physical wave dynamics through discrete bit-shift registers. When you integrate nanosecond optical crossbars on microchannel diamond interposers, the distinction between memory access and logical execution dissolves completely. Light routes matrix math directly through the physical medium 💡.

We don't need incremental software patches for memory bottlenecks. We need hardware-software co-design that treats heat dissipation, photonics, and memory structures as a single standing wave. The operators who win the next decade won't be those buying the most accelerators, but those who collapse the thermodynamic tax on data movement 📈.

Are you still scaling planar copper interconnects, or are you preparing for substrate-native wave execution?

I am an investor who has had to work really hard to learn the semi space. For that reason, among others, I find your Substack to be invaluable.

With that said, I do lead an investment group where we do a LOT of research to build conviction within sectors as well as among specific companies.

The framework I approach it from is based on my studies of elite traders who have built fortunes in the stock market.

Basically, I am looking for a structural trend that I can ride through the greater part of its move.

If I can be right about the structural move, my biggest task as a stock operator is to have the emotional discipline to manage the campaigns (we call them campaigns and not trades) through the volatility.

From my experience, that is where the big money is made.

In addition, we are not against adding 'trading shares' in these companies that can be acquired during drawdowns (the "buy opportunities" you referenced) as long as the structural uptrend is still in tact and the longer-term line of least resistance is higher.

These trading shares can be sold for profit when the aggregate market, the sector or individual stocks get extended (we monitor charts constantly to determine those situations).

While position sizing can vary depending on the near-term line of least resistance in the overall market, the sector or the stock, IMHO the key is to have the emotional mastery to hold the core position without trying to time tops and bottoms.

IMO, picking tops and bottoms in a really tough game and you often risk missing the greater move if you don't time it correctly.

That is why we say if you want to partake in that exercise then use trading shares and not your core positions.

In the case of the current AI cycle, we have advocated holding core positions in key names we have identified and the key "tell" as to whether or not the structural trend remains in tact is the CapEx spending of the bigger companies.

This is something we monitor rigorously and with great vigilance because when that spending decelerates then the overall thesis changes and the structural trend is invalidated.

At the end of the day the following quote attributed to Jesse Livermore substantiates this approach:

"It never was my thinking that made the big money for me. It always was my sitting. Got that? My sitting tight!...I've known many men who were right at exactly the right time, and began buying or selling stocks when prices were at the very level which should show the greatest profit. And their experience invariably matched mine--that is, they made no real money out of it. Men who can both be right and sit tight are uncommon.”

Just my 2 cents and my apologies for the long post.

items.question:
While the historical scaling curve of 10x to 100x parameter growth per generation has ended, total parameter counts will continue expanding through massive Mixture of Experts (MoE) routing. This systemic parameter expansion directly undermines the core value proposition of wafer-scale architectures like Cerebras.

Once a majority of MoE models outgrow the 44 GB on-chip SRAM boundary, Cerebras cannot sustain real-time inference by relying on external memory alone. Because the external connection to MemoryX is too slow to support real-time token generation, the architecture increasingly requires pipeline parallelism across multiple clustered wafers.

Silicon physics offers no viable escape from this memory bottleneck. The physical SRAM wall firmly restricts 2D on-wafer capacity; migrating a maximum-reticle 300mm wafer to advanced 2nm or 14A nodes will realistically yield only 53 GB to 55 GB of total SRAM. Furthermore, attempting to bypass this limit via 3D wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding remains structurally unfeasible. Stacking two 300mm wafers compounds the unique microscopic defect maps of each silicon layer, which would catastrophically reduce functional yield. Additionally, vertical silicon stacking creates severe thermal isolation, physically separating the lower wafer from the microfluidic cooling required to dissipate the immense heat generated by wafer-scale compute.

For single-user deployment, Cerebras is vulnerable to the Innovator’s Dilemma. Edge compute has reached a point where wafer-scale bandwidth is increasingly unnecessary. Existing consumer hardware, such as the 2021 M1 Max MacBook Pro with 400 GB/s of memory bandwidth and 64 GB of on-chip RAM, already provides sufficient throughput to serve inference for a 44–55 GB MoE model.
